newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Defiant IRA says Britain must drop talks bar.
newsitem.headline: Defiant IRA says Britain must drop talks bar.

text.p: IRA guerrillas said on Wednesday they wanted a voice in all-party Northern Ireland peace talks but signalled they would keep on fighting until Britain issues an unconditional inviation to take part.

"We approach the year ahead unified, confident and steadfast in our commitment to succeed," said Irish Republican Army commanders, declaring that their primary objective was a reunited Ireland free of British influence.
The statement, released to Irish media ahead of publication on Thursday in An Phoblacht, the weekly paper of its Sinn Fein political arm, was the movement's first declaration this year.
The IRA castigated Britain's handling of peace efforts that collapsed when the guerrillas ended a 17-month truce last February with a huge bomb in eastern London.

"No amount of British obduracy will deflect us from the task we have set ourselves," said the statement, issued just days before resumption of multi-party talks in Belfast from which Sinn Fein is excluded.
The guerrillas' blunt words followed two rocket and mortar attacks on police in British-ruled Northern Ireland.

British security officials said the incidents, which have fuelled fears of a backlash by pro-British Loyalist extremists, were further proof of a return to old-style IRA violence alongside stalled efforts to revive the province's peace hopes.
Britain says it will not permit the IRA to bomb its way into peace talks and insists the guerrillas must call a genuine cessation of violence before Sinn Fein is allowed to the table.
Sinn Fein, which won 15.5 per cent of the vote in a province- wide election last June, says it has a democratic right to be in talks. London insists the IRA must abandon violence first.

In its statement, the IRA said it was committed to the establishment of "a just and lasting peace in Ireland" and commended efforts by others to put together "a meaningful process" aimed at securing a lasting peace settlement.
"Lasting peace requires an inclusive negotiated settlement. There can be no preconditions on participation in such negotiations," the IRA asserted.
Britain says the 17-month truce called in 1994 was phoney and that the guerrillas used it to prepare for the resumption of bombings.
The IRA accused British Prime John Major of squandering the opportunity for stability presented by its ceasefire.

The guerrillas, who see themselves as inheritors of a 70 year old struggle to reunite Ireland against the wishes of Northern Ireland's pro-British Protestant majority, said Britain lacked the will to build a meaningful peace process.
Pro-British Loyalist militants are widely suspected of two recent attacks on senior republicans but parties close to the Loyalist fighters insist that their 26-month-old truce is still on.
Britain, under Protestant political pressure for tougher security measures, said on Wednesday extremists would be hunted and put behind bars.
